stages.title: Multiphysics engineering analysis
stages.hook: An electric motor housing heats up from its windings, expands, changes the air gap and so changes the magnetic and heating behaviour in turn. How do you analyse a system where the physics feed back on each other?
explain: Many real problems couple several physical fields: thermal with structural (thermal stress), fluid with structure (aeroelasticity), electrical with thermal (Joule heating) and chemical with thermal. A multiphysics model solves the governing equations of each field together or in sequence. The central modelling decision is the coupling: one-way (field A drives B, with no feedback) or two-way, solved either monolithically (one big system) or by staggered iteration between solvers.

A simple coupled estimate is thermal stress. A bar of length L free to expand lengthens by ΔL = α L ΔT. For steel with α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, L = 2 m and ΔT = 50 K, ΔL = 1.2 mm. If the bar is fully constrained, the stress is σ = E α ΔT = 200 × 10⁹ × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = 120 MPa (compressive on heating), which can buckle slender members or crush joints.

Time and length scales decide how to couple. For a lumped thermal body, the time constant is τ = ρ c V ÷ (h A). For a steel plate of effective thickness V ÷ A = 0.01 m, ρ = 7800 kg/m³, c = 500 J/(kg K) and h = 50 W/(m² K): τ = 7800 × 500 × 0.01 ÷ 50 = 780 s. The lumped approximation is valid when the Biot number Bi = h L ÷ k is below about 0.1; with k = 50 W/(m K) and L = 0.01 m, Bi = 0.01. Joule heating in a conductor is P = I² R: 100 A through 0.002 Ω dissipates 20 W.

Credible multiphysics work needs verification of each single-physics model first, then of the coupling (check energy balance and conservation across interfaces), then validation against measurements. Common failure causes are mismatched meshes at interfaces, inconsistent units, using one-way coupling when feedback is strong, and unconverged coupling iterations. Safety link: thermal runaway in batteries is a coupled electro-thermal-chemical process, so design relies on conservative models and tests, not on a single simulation.

example.q: A steel member (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) is rigidly fixed at both ends and warms by 50 K. Find the thermal stress.
steps: Free expansion strain would be α ΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = 6 × 10⁻⁴.
The constraint prevents it, so the elastic strain is −6 × 10⁻⁴.
σ = E × strain = 200 × 10⁹ × 6 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.2 × 10⁸ Pa = 120 MPa, compressive.

analogies.home: A pan of hot oil heats the handle, which then warms your hand: heat links the pieces in a chain.
analogies.city: Railway tracks expand in summer heat and can buckle if no gaps are left.
analogies.farm: A greenhouse's glass, air, plants and sun interact: heat, humidity and growth are linked.
analogies.tech: A phone gets hot while charging, which changes the battery's performance, which changes the heat.

stages.mnemonic: Couple the fields, check the scales, conserve at the interface.
terms: Analysis of two or more interacting physical phenomena.
One field drives another with no feedback.
Stress from constrained thermal expansion, σ = E α ΔT.
h L ÷ k, comparing surface heat transfer to internal conduction.

misc.wrong: Running separate simulations of each physics and combining the pictures is the same as a coupled analysis.
misc.right: If the fields feed back on each other, the answers change when solved together; interface conservation and iteration to convergence are needed.

stages.limits: Coupled models need material data that vary with temperature and field, and uncertainty in those data can dominate the answer.

trip.prompt: Find an example of a coupled problem such as thermal-structural. Which direction is the coupling?

questions.q: What distinguishes two-way from one-way coupling?
o: Both fields influence each other
Only one equation is used for both fields
It requires no mesh at the interface at all
It never needs any iteration between the solvers
questions.why: Feedback in both directions is two-way coupling.

questions.q: A steel rod (α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) of length 2 m is heated by 50 K and is free to expand. What is the extension in millimetres?
Aluminium (E = 70 GPa, α = 23 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹) is fully constrained and heated by 40 K. What is the compressive stress in MPa?
A steel plate has ρ = 7800 kg/m³, c = 500 J/(kg K), V ÷ A = 0.01 m and h = 50 W/(m² K). What is its lumped thermal time constant in seconds?
The Biot number of a body is 2. What does this imply about a lumped-temperature model?
o: It is invalid because internal temperature differences matter
It is exact, because the temperature is then uniform
Conduction in the body is effectively infinite
Convection at the surface is zero
questions.why: Bi greater than about 0.1 means conduction inside is not fast compared to surface transfer.

questions.q: Two codes are coupled and the exchanged heat flux at an interface does not conserve energy between them. What is the likely cause?
o: Mismatched interface mapping or meshes
Perfect coupling, so the mismatch must be harmless
Too small a mesh at the interface
A negative absolute temperature in one code
questions.why: Interpolation between non-matching meshes can lose or create flux unless conservative mapping is used.

questions.q: A battery pack design is validated only with a one-way electrical to thermal model. When is this dangerous?
o: When temperature changes resistance and heating strongly (feedback)
When the pack is cold and makes almost no heat, since all models are risky then
When there is no heat
Never
questions.why: Thermal runaway is a positive-feedback process, which one-way coupling cannot capture.

questions.q: Why are long railway rails welded with expansion allowances or pre-tensioned?
o: To avoid buckling from thermal compressive stress
To make noise that warns of approaching trains
To save steel only, with no effect on stress
To reduce friction between the rail and the wheels
questions.why: Constrained rails develop large compressive stress in summer.

questions.q: Describe a sound verification and validation sequence for a coupled thermal-structural simulation of an engine component.
questions.model: First verify each single-physics model against hand calculations, then check that the coupling conserves energy at interfaces and that coupling iterations and mesh refinement converge. Finally validate against measurements such as thermocouple and strain-gauge data.
questions.why: Errors are isolated by building confidence in layers.

questions.q: Match each coupled example to its fields.
questions.why: Each example shows which physics interact.

panel.q: A solver uses staggered coupling and the results change when the time step is halved. What does that show?
o: Splitting error from lagging the coupling is significant
The physics is wrong, since a good model cannot depend on the time step
Time steps are irrelevant
The mesh is perfect
panel.why: Lagging the exchange adds time-step-dependent error; sub-iterations or smaller steps reduce it.

panel.q: The thermal conductivity data used in a model came from room temperature, but the part runs at 600 °C. What is the sensible action?
o: Use temperature-dependent data and quantify uncertainty
Ignore the difference, since conductivity hardly changes
Use the room-temperature value anyway
Remove conduction from the model to avoid the problem
panel.why: Material properties vary with temperature, and stale data can bias the whole coupled result.

panel.q: A claim states a coupled simulation 'proves' a design safe. What is the best response?
o: Ask for validation, uncertainty bounds and independent checks
Accept it, since the simulation is detailed enough
Reject all simulation as unreliable
Increase the mesh density only and accept the result
panel.why: Simulation supports but does not replace validated evidence for safety decisions.

teach.topic: Why coupled physics must sometimes be solved together
teach.model: When two physical effects affect each other, such as heat changing size and size changing heat flow, solving them separately can give the wrong answer. A multiphysics model exchanges information between the fields, either in one solver or by iterating between solvers. Engineers verify each physics, check conservation at the interface and validate with measurements.

points.ask: What makes a problem multiphysics?
How are they solved?
What must you check at the interface?
How do you trust the result, and what is an example?

stages.title: Advanced structural simulation
stages.hook: A slender column carries a load far below the material's strength, yet it suddenly bows sideways and collapses. How can a simulation predict that, and what must it include?
explain: Advanced structural simulation extends linear static FEA to dynamics, stability and extreme events. Four analysis types matter most: modal (natural frequencies and mode shapes), buckling (loss of stability), transient dynamics and nonlinear analysis (material, geometric and contact).

Euler buckling for a slender column gives the critical load Pcr = π² E I ÷ (K L)², where K depends on end conditions (1 for pinned-pinned, 2 for fixed-free). For a steel column (E = 200 GPa) of diameter 20 mm, I = π d⁴ ÷ 64 = 7.85 × 10⁻⁹ m⁴. With L = 1 m and pinned ends, Pcr = 9.87 × 200 × 10⁹ × 7.85 × 10⁻⁹ = 15.5 kN. Fixed-free (K = 2) gives one quarter, 3.9 kN. Buckling depends on stiffness, not strength; imperfections and nonlinearity lower the real load.

Modal analysis gives the natural frequencies, such as for a cantilever f₁ = (1.875² ÷ 2π) √(E I ÷ (ρ A L⁴)). For the same 20 mm steel rod as a 0.5 m cantilever (ρ = 7850 kg/m³, A = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m²), f₁ ≈ 56.5 Hz. Frequencies drive the avoidance of resonance and the choice of dynamic method.

Explicit dynamics suits impacts and crashes with small time steps limited by the stability condition Δt ≤ Lₑ ÷ c, where c = √(E ÷ ρ) is the wave speed. For steel c = 5050 m/s, so with a 5 mm element Δt ≈ 1 μs. Implicit methods take larger steps but must solve equations at each step. Good practice includes sensitivity to imperfections, mesh and time-step convergence, correct contact and constraints, and comparison with hand estimates and tests. Responsible use means not trusting a buckling load without knockdown factors for imperfections.

example.q: A pinned-pinned steel column (E = 200 GPa) has a solid circular section of 20 mm diameter and is 1 m long. Find the Euler critical load.
steps: Pcr = π² E I ÷ (K L)² with K = 1, L = 1 m.

analogies.home: A thin plastic ruler squeezed end to end suddenly bows sideways long before it crushes.
analogies.city: Tall slender towers and bridge piers are checked for stability as well as strength.
analogies.farm: A long thin fence post under a heavy load can bend sideways rather than crush.
analogies.sea: A ship's thin hull plates can buckle under compressive wave loads.

stages.mnemonic: Strength crushes, stiffness buckles: check both, then dynamics.
terms: Finding natural frequencies and mode shapes.
Time stepping without solving a global system, limited by a small stable step.
A reduction to account for imperfections in theoretical buckling loads.

misc.wrong: A column fails only when stress reaches the material's yield strength.
misc.right: Slender columns buckle at a load set by stiffness and geometry, often much lower than the crushing load.

stages.limits: Classical Euler buckling assumes perfect, elastic, straight columns. Real columns have imperfections, plasticity and eccentric loads.

trip.prompt: Find the Euler buckling formula and the effective length factors for different end conditions.

questions.q: Which property mainly controls Euler buckling load of a slender column?
o: Stiffness (E I) and length
Yield strength only, whatever the length
The colour of the coating on the column
Density only, as it sets the weight
questions.why: Pcr = π² E I ÷ (K L)², so it depends on bending stiffness and effective length.

questions.q: A pinned-pinned steel column (E = 200 GPa) has I = 7.854 × 10⁻⁹ m⁴ and L = 1 m. What is the Euler load in kN? Use π² = 9.87.
The same column is fixed at the base and free at the top (K = 2). What is the Euler load in kN?
For steel, E = 200 GPa and ρ = 7850 kg/m³. What is the elastic wave speed √(E ÷ ρ) in m/s? Round to the nearest 10.
An explicit dynamic model uses 5 mm elements in steel. About what is the stable time step?
o: About 1 microsecond
About 1 second
About 1 millisecond
About 1 minute

questions.q: Why does halving the length of a pinned column raise its Euler load fourfold?
o: Pcr ∝ 1 ÷ L²
Pcr ∝ L
Pcr ∝ 1 ÷ L
Pcr is independent of length
questions.why: Length appears squared in the denominator.

questions.q: A tested thin cylinder buckles at 60% of the theoretical load. What explains this?
o: Geometric imperfections reduce the buckling load
The theory is exact, so the test must be faulty
Steel is always weaker than the tables suggest
The cylinder is too short for the theory
questions.why: Shell buckling is highly imperfection-sensitive, so knockdown factors are used.

questions.q: A linear buckling analysis predicts a safe load factor of 1.5 for a shell. What is the responsible action?
o: Include imperfections and nonlinear analysis, and apply knockdown factors
Accept 1.5 as a safe load factor, since linear analysis already includes everything
Double the load
Ignore stability
questions.why: Linear eigenvalue buckling is non-conservative for imperfection-sensitive structures.

questions.q: Explain why a modal analysis is carried out before choosing the loading frequency range for a transient simulation.
questions.model: Modal analysis reveals the natural frequencies and mode shapes. It shows whether the loading can excite resonance and which frequencies the time step and mesh must resolve.
questions.why: It guides both the physics expectations and numerical settings.

questions.q: Match each analysis to its purpose.
questions.why: Each analysis answers a different design question.

panel.q: A column of 1 m length and 20 mm diameter is replaced by a 40 mm diameter column. How does the Euler load change?
o: It rises sixteen times
It rises four times, in line with the diameter squared
It doubles, in line with the diameter
It rises eight times, in line with the diameter cubed
panel.why: I ∝ d⁴, so doubling d gives 2⁴ = 16.

panel.q: Mesh refinement shows the first natural frequency changing by 0.2% while stresses change by 12%. What can you conclude?
o: The frequency has converged but the stress has not
All results have converged, since the frequency has
Neither has converged, as both changed
The model is invalid and must be rebuilt
panel.why: Derived quantities such as local stresses converge more slowly than global ones.

panel.q: A footbridge's first vertical mode is near 2 Hz, close to walking pace. What is the design concern?
o: Resonant vibration from pedestrian loading, affecting comfort and safety
Corrosion of the steel and wear of the bearings are the only real worries
None
Aesthetic only
panel.why: Pedestrian frequencies of 1.5 to 2.5 Hz can excite lively bridges; codes require checks.

teach.topic: Why a slender column can buckle below its crushing load
teach.model: A slender column under compression can suddenly bow sideways when the load reaches a critical value that depends on its stiffness and length, not its strength. The Euler load is π² E I ÷ (K L)². Halving the length makes it four times larger. Real columns buckle earlier because of imperfections, so engineers apply knockdown factors.

points.ask: What kind of member buckles?
What decides the buckling load?
Is it about strength?
Why do real columns buckle earlier?

stages.title: Turbulence and complex fluid systems
stages.hook: Stir milk into coffee: it forms swirls of every size, from the cup scale down to tiny filaments. How small do the smallest swirls get, and what would it cost to simulate every one?
explain: Turbulence is chaotic three-dimensional flow with eddies over a wide range of scales. Energy enters at large scales, cascades to smaller eddies and is dissipated by viscosity at the Kolmogorov scale η = (ν³ ÷ ε)^(1/4), where ν is kinematic viscosity and ε the dissipation rate per unit mass. For water (ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s) with ε = 1 m²/s³, η = (10⁻¹⁸)^(1/4) = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ m.

Resolving all scales (DNS) needs about Re^(9/4) grid points in three dimensions. At Re = 10⁴ that is 10⁹ points; at 10⁶ it is 3 × 10¹³. This is why industry uses RANS models and sometimes LES. Key turbulence quantities: turbulent kinetic energy k = ½(u′² + v′² + w′²) (for fluctuation rms values 0.5, 0.4 and 0.3 m/s, k = 0.25 m²/s²) and turbulence intensity I = u′ ÷ U (0.5 ÷ 10 = 5%).

Near walls the friction velocity uτ = √(τw ÷ ρ) sets the scale. With τw = 2 Pa in water, uτ = 0.0447 m/s, and a point 1 mm from the wall has y⁺ = y uτ ÷ ν = 44.7. Wall functions are valid for y⁺ roughly 30 to 300; resolving the viscous sublayer needs y⁺ near 1.

Complex fluids add more difficulty. Non-Newtonian fluids have shear-dependent viscosity, for example the power law μ = K γ̇ⁿ⁻¹; with K = 2 Pa sⁿ, n = 0.5 and γ̇ = 100 s⁻¹, μ = 0.2 Pa s. Multiphase flow (bubbles, sprays, slurries) and compressible turbulence need extra models. Honest practice includes showing grid and model sensitivity, comparing with benchmarks and stating uncertainty. Safety link: turbulent loads cause flow-induced vibration of pipes and heat exchanger tubes, which fatigue them.

example.q: Water (ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s) has a turbulent dissipation rate ε = 1 m²/s³. Find the Kolmogorov length scale.

analogies.home: Smoke from a candle rises smoothly, then breaks into swirls of many sizes.
analogies.city: River flow around bridge piers forms eddies that scour the bed.
analogies.farm: Wind through a crop field makes gusts at many scales.
analogies.sea: Ship wakes show large vortices breaking into smaller ones.

stages.mnemonic: Big eddies feed small eddies, viscosity eats the smallest.
terms: Smallest turbulent length scale where viscosity dissipates energy.
Energy per unit mass in velocity fluctuations.
Dimensionless distance from a wall in wall units.
A fluid whose viscosity depends on the rate of shear.

misc.wrong: Turbulence is random noise that cannot be modelled.
misc.right: Turbulence is deterministic but chaotic. Its statistics follow patterns and models capture them with limits.

stages.limits: Turbulence models are empirical, and no single model works for all flows. Separation, rotation and strong curvature are challenging.

trip.prompt: Find the energy cascade diagram. Where are energy-containing eddies, the inertial range and dissipation?

questions.q: At which scale is turbulent energy mainly dissipated into heat?
o: The smallest (Kolmogorov) scale
The largest eddies, which carry the flow energy
The pipe diameter of the system
The mesh size used in the model
questions.why: Viscosity acts strongly on the smallest eddies.

questions.q: A turbulent flow has fluctuation rms values u′ = 0.5, v′ = 0.4 and w′ = 0.3 m/s. What is the turbulent kinetic energy k = ½(u′² + v′² + w′²) in m²/s²?
The wall shear stress in water is 2 Pa (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s). What is y⁺ at 1 mm from the wall? Round to one decimal place.
A shear-thinning fluid follows μ = K γ̇ⁿ⁻¹ with K = 2 Pa sⁿ and n = 0.5. What is the apparent viscosity at γ̇ = 100 s⁻¹ in Pa s?
How does the number of DNS grid points scale with Reynolds number in 3D?
o: About Re^(9/4)
About Re
About Re^(1/2)
Independent of Re
questions.why: Resolving the full range of scales needs Re^(9/4) points.

questions.q: Why can't DNS be used for a full-size aircraft wing in design?
o: The number of grid points required is far beyond computing capacity
DNS is inaccurate for every flow, so engineers never use it for any wing
Wings are too small
DNS needs no mesh
questions.why: Re of 10⁷ or more gives astronomically many points.

questions.q: A heat exchanger tube bundle cracks near supports after months. What flow-related mechanism is likely?
o: Flow-induced vibration causing fatigue and fretting
Cavitation of the air in the shell
Static overload from the weight of the tubes
Frozen water blocking the tubes
questions.why: Turbulent buffeting and vortex shedding excite tubes, causing fretting wear and fatigue.

questions.q: An LES case shows large changes when the filter width is halved. What does this suggest?
o: The grid is too coarse to resolve the energy-containing eddies
The grid is perfect and the change is only random noise in the solver
LES doesn't depend on grid
The Reynolds number is zero
questions.why: A good LES resolves most turbulent energy so results are not sensitive to the filter.

questions.q: Explain the energy cascade in turbulence in a few sentences.
questions.model: Energy enters turbulence at large scales and is passed to smaller and smaller eddies through breakup, with little loss in the inertial range. At the smallest (Kolmogorov) scales viscosity converts the energy into heat.
questions.why: The cascade explains why small scales need modelling or fine grids.

questions.q: Match each approach to its feature.
questions.why: Cost and fidelity trade off between these approaches.

panel.q: A pipe flow of toothpaste-like fluid seems to flow only above a minimum stress. What property is this?
o: Yield stress (Bingham-type behaviour)
Turbulence caused by the high speed
Cavitation from low pressure
Compressibility of the fluid
panel.why: Some fluids behave as solids until a yield stress is exceeded.

panel.q: A CFD team reports one RANS model result with no sensitivity study. What is the best critique?
o: Model-form uncertainty is not quantified; compare models and meshes
None; one RANS model is the industry standard and needs no comparison
Add colours
Run fewer cases
panel.why: Different turbulence models can disagree, especially in separated flow.

panel.q: Doubling Re in a flow raises DNS cost by how much compared with DNS count of grid points alone?
o: About 4.8 times in points
Twice as many points, in step with Re
Half as many points, since cells get larger
No change at all, as the mesh does not depend on Re
panel.why: 2^(9/4) is about 4.76 times as many points (and more total cost, since time steps also rise).

teach.topic: Why turbulence is so costly to simulate
teach.model: Turbulence has eddies from the size of the flow down to tiny scales where viscosity dissipates the energy. Resolving them all needs a number of grid points that grows like Re to the power 9/4, which is impossible at engineering Reynolds numbers. So we model the small scales (LES) or all of them (RANS), and accept modelling uncertainty.

points.ask: What is in a turbulent flow?
How does energy move between scales?
Why can't we just simulate everything?
What do engineers do instead?

stages.title: Nonlinear mechanical behaviour
stages.hook: A paper clip bent a little springs back; bent more, it stays bent; a rubber band stretches ten times its length. Why can't one linear stiffness describe them all?
explain: Linear analysis assumes small displacements, linear elastic materials and fixed boundary conditions. Real behaviour departs from this in three ways: material nonlinearity (plasticity, hyperelasticity, creep), geometric nonlinearity (large displacement, buckling) and boundary nonlinearity (contact, friction). Each can change the stiffness during loading.

Plasticity: a bilinear steel with E = 200 GPa, yield 250 MPa and tangent modulus Et = 2 GPa yields at strain 0.00125. At a total strain of 0.005, the plastic part is 0.00375 and the stress is 250 + 2000 × 0.00375 = 257.5 MPa. Large-strain work uses true values: σtrue = σeng (1 + εeng) and εtrue = ln(1 + εeng). At engineering stress 400 MPa and strain 0.10, σtrue = 440 MPa and εtrue = 0.0953.

Hyperelastic materials like rubber store energy elastically at large strain. For an incompressible neo-Hookean solid in uniaxial stretch λ, σ = μ(λ² − 1 ÷ λ). With μ = 0.5 MPa and λ = 2, σ = 0.5 × (4 − 0.5) = 1.75 MPa. Creep is time-dependent deformation; Norton's law ε̇ = A σⁿ means that with n = 5, doubling the stress raises the creep rate 2⁵ = 32 times.

Nonlinear problems are solved incrementally with Newton–Raphson iteration, which converges quadratically near the solution but can fail near snap-through, contact changes or softening. Good practice is small load steps, line search or arc-length methods, checking energy balance, and comparing with simple tests. The consequence of ignoring nonlinearity is serious: a linear model may predict safe stresses when plastic collapse, snap-through or contact loss is real.

example.q: Steel with E = 200 GPa, yield stress 250 MPa and tangent modulus 2 GPa is strained to 0.005. What is the stress?

analogies.home: Bending a spoon a little returns, but bending far leaves a permanent bend.
analogies.city: A bridge bearing that lifts off and re-contacts the pier changes the structure's stiffness.
analogies.farm: A rubber hose stretches far more with little force at first, then stiffens.
analogies.sport: A diving board stiffens as it bends further because of geometry.

stages.mnemonic: Material, geometry, contact: three roads to nonlinear.
terms: Large-strain elastic behaviour of rubber-like materials.
Iterative method that linearises the problem at each step.

misc.wrong: If the linear stress is below yield, the nonlinear result will be about the same.
misc.right: Large displacement, contact and local plasticity can redistribute loads, so linear results may be unconservative or wrong.

stages.limits: Nonlinear material models need calibrated data from tests, and solutions can be non-unique, with different load paths giving different answers.

trip.prompt: Find a stress-strain curve with elastic and plastic regions. Where would a bilinear model approximate it?

questions.q: Which is a geometric nonlinearity?
o: Large deflection changing the stiffness
Yielding of the steel under load
Contact between the parts of the assembly
Rubber stretching under a heavy pull
questions.why: When displacements are large, the geometry changes the load path.

questions.q: A steel with E = 200 GPa, σy = 250 MPa and tangent modulus 2 GPa is strained to 0.006. What is the stress in MPa?
A specimen reaches engineering stress 400 MPa at engineering strain 0.10. What is the true stress in MPa (assuming constant volume)?
An incompressible neo-Hookean rubber has μ = 0.5 MPa and is stretched uniaxially to λ = 2. What is the (Cauchy) stress in MPa?
A creep law ε̇ = A σⁿ has n = 5. The stress rises by 20%. By what factor does the creep rate increase?
o: About 2.5
About 1.2, the same as the rise in stress
About 5, equal to the exponent n
About 1.0, with no increase at all

questions.q: A Newton–Raphson solution fails to converge as a shallow arch snaps through. What is a suitable remedy?
o: Use arc-length control or smaller steps
Increase the load step to jump over the snap
Switch to a linear analysis for the whole arch
Remove the boundary conditions from the model
questions.why: Load control cannot follow limit points; arc-length methods trace the full path.

questions.q: A linear analysis shows a bracket stress of 180 MPa, below the 250 MPa yield. Contact at a pin is modelled as bonded. Why might this be unsafe?
o: The real contact can open or slide and raise local stress
Bonded contact is always the safe, conservative choice for any pin joint
Pins carry no load
Contact removes stress
questions.why: Contact nonlinearity can concentrate loads in ways bonded models miss.

questions.q: Why does a rubber seal's stiffness increase at large compression?
o: Material and geometric stiffening at large strain
It turns into steel when it is squeezed hard
Its mass increases as it is compressed
It moves into the linear range at large strain
questions.why: Hyperelastic response and contact make the force-deflection curve rise steeply.

questions.q: A designer uses a linear elastic model to approve a ductile steel bracket whose peak stress is 30% above yield at a notch. Argue for or against approval and justify it.
questions.model: A locally yielded notch in a ductile steel does not automatically mean failure, since plasticity redistributes load. But linear stress cannot show strains or whether repeated loading causes ratcheting or fatigue, so a nonlinear elastic-plastic analysis and a fatigue check are needed before approval.
questions.why: Linear results beyond yield are not meaningful quantitatively.

questions.q: Match each nonlinearity to an example.
pairs: Large deflection of a thin plate
questions.why: Each type changes the response in a different way.

panel.q: An elastic-perfectly plastic beam reaches full plastic hinge at a bending moment higher than first yield. What is the ratio called for a rectangle?
o: Shape factor of 1.5
A factor of 0.5, since the section is half used
A factor of 3, as the moment is tripled
Equal to one, since the beam yields at once
panel.why: The plastic moment is 1.5 times the first yield moment for a rectangular section.

panel.q: After a part is loaded beyond yield and unloaded, what remains?
o: Residual stresses and permanent strain
Nothing remains once the load is taken off
A higher modulus only, with no strain left
Zero strain, as the part springs back fully
panel.why: Plastic deformation leaves residual strain and stress, which affect later fatigue and distortion.

panel.q: A nonlinear model gives different results depending on the order loads are applied. What does that indicate?
o: Path dependence, as in plasticity and friction
A mistake in the software, always
Linear superposition holds, so order should matter little
Gravity is absent from the model
panel.why: Plastic and frictional responses depend on history, so the load sequence must be modelled.

teach.model: A linear model assumes constant stiffness, small movements and fixed supports. Real structures can yield, deflect far, or make and lose contact, so stiffness changes as loading proceeds. Nonlinear solvers apply the load in steps and iterate, using methods such as Newton–Raphson. Ignoring nonlinearity can hide collapse or snap-through.

points.ask: What does a linear model assume?
How does reality differ?
How is it solved?
What could go wrong if you ignore it?

stages.title: Advanced thermal-fluid systems
stages.hook: A power plant turns fuel heat into electricity, then discards most of it. Where does it go, and how do heat exchangers and cycle design decide how much is wasted?
explain: Thermal-fluid systems combine thermodynamic cycles, heat exchangers and fluid machinery. In a Rankine steam cycle a pump raises the pressure of liquid water, a boiler adds heat, a turbine extracts work and a condenser rejects heat. Efficiency η = (w_turbine − w_pump) ÷ q_in. For w_turbine = 1000 kJ/kg, w_pump = 10 kJ/kg and q_in = 3000 kJ/kg, η = 990 ÷ 3000 = 33%. Higher boiler temperature, lower condenser pressure and reheating raise efficiency, within material and moisture limits.

Heat exchanger design uses Q = U A ΔT_lm, where U is the overall coefficient, A the area and ΔT_lm the log-mean temperature difference: ΔT_lm = (ΔT₁ − ΔT₂) ÷ ln(ΔT₁ ÷ ΔT₂). With ΔT₁ = 60 K and ΔT₂ = 20 K, ΔT_lm = 40 ÷ 1.0986 = 36.4 K. For U = 500 W/(m² K) and A = 2 m², Q = 36.4 kW. The effectiveness–NTU method is used when outlet temperatures are unknown; with a condensing or boiling stream (capacity ratio zero), ε = 1 − e^(−NTU), so NTU = 1 gives 63.2%.

Refrigeration and heat pumps move heat against its natural direction using work. The coefficient of performance COP = Q_cold ÷ W for cooling. The ideal limit is Carnot COP = Tc ÷ (Th − Tc). For a cold space at 268 K and surroundings at 303 K, COP_Carnot = 268 ÷ 35 = 7.66; real systems reach perhaps half of this.

Design decisions trade capital cost, efficiency, size, fouling and safety. Fouling raises thermal resistance over time, and pressure drop raises pumping power. Safety and environmental points: high-pressure steam and refrigerants need relief devices and inspection; refrigerants with high global warming potential are being replaced; waste heat can be recovered by combined heat and power or organic Rankine cycles.

stages.title: Intelligent manufacturing
stages.hook: A vision system flags defective parts with 95% sensitivity and a 5% false alarm rate, yet only 1 part in 100 is actually defective. If it flags a part, how likely is the part to be truly defective?
explain: Intelligent manufacturing connects sensors, networks, data analytics and automation so a factory can sense, decide and adapt. Typical elements are machine data collection (for example through OPC UA or MQTT), edge computing near the machine, cloud analytics, machine learning and feedback into the process. Industry 4.0 and Industry 5.0 describe these trends, the latter adding human-centric and sustainability goals.

Machine learning for quality inspection must be judged with the right metrics. From a confusion matrix with true positives TP, false positives FP and false negatives FN: precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP), recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN) and F1 = 2PR ÷ (P + R). With TP = 90, FP = 10 and FN = 30, precision = 0.90, recall = 0.75 and F1 = 0.818.

Base rates matter. By Bayes' theorem, P(defect | alarm) = P(alarm | defect) P(defect) ÷ P(alarm). With sensitivity 0.95, false-alarm rate 0.05 and defect rate 0.01: 0.95 × 0.01 = 0.0095 true alarms, 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.0495 false alarms, so P = 0.0095 ÷ 0.0590 = 16.1%. Most alarms are false, so a second check or a better model is needed.

Design and governance decisions: models must be validated on new data, monitored for drift when materials or lighting change, and given a safe fallback. Cybersecurity is a safety matter: a networked machine can be attacked, so networks are segmented and access controlled. Human issues are real: transparency to workers, avoiding unfair surveillance, retraining and keeping humans accountable for safety-critical decisions. Machine learning should not be used to override mandatory safety functions.

stages.title: Autonomous robotics
stages.hook: A warehouse robot must find its way, avoid people and keep track of its own position using noisy sensors. How can it combine imperfect information into a confident estimate?
explain: An autonomous robot cycles through sensing, estimation, planning and control. Sensors include encoders, inertial units, lidar, cameras and ultrasonic devices, each with noise and failure modes. Estimation fuses them to track the state (position, heading, velocity) with uncertainty.

The Kalman filter combines a prediction with a measurement, weighting by their uncertainties. In one dimension, with prior variance P and measurement variance R, the gain is K = P ÷ (P + R). With P = 4 and R = 1, K = 0.8. If the predicted position is x = 10 and the measurement is z = 12, the update is x̂ = 10 + 0.8 × (12 − 10) = 11.6 and the new variance is (1 − K) P = 0.8, smaller than either input.

Kinematics of a differential-drive robot: forward speed v = (v_r + v_l) ÷ 2 and turn rate ω = (v_r − v_l) ÷ L, where L is wheel separation. With v_r = 0.6, v_l = 0.4 m/s and L = 0.4 m, v = 0.5 m/s, ω = 0.5 rad/s and turning radius v ÷ ω = 1 m. Path planning searches a map for a collision-free route, for example with A*, which uses a cost-to-go heuristic, while local planners react to moving obstacles.

Safety is decisive. The stopping distance must fit within the sensing range: d = v t_r + v² ÷ (2a). For v = 2 m/s, a reaction time of 0.2 s and deceleration of 1 m/s², d = 0.4 + 2 = 2.4 m. Standards such as ISO 13482 (personal care robots) and ISO 3691-4 (driverless industrial trucks) call for hazard analysis, safe stopping and emergency stops. Failure causes include sensor blinding, localisation loss, software faults and unexpected human behaviour. Responsible design keeps humans able to intervene, logs decisions and tests in simulation and in controlled trials before public deployment.

stages.title: Digital twins and predictive maintenance
stages.hook: A pump on a remote offshore platform hums slightly differently each week. How can a computer model of it, fed with live sensor data, warn of failure before anyone climbs aboard?
explain: A digital twin is a virtual model of a physical asset, kept in step with it by live data and used for monitoring, prediction and what-if tests. It may combine physics-based models, data-driven models and the asset's maintenance history. The loop is: sense, update the model, predict, decide and act on the real machine.

Predictive maintenance estimates remaining useful life (RUL). If a health index falls linearly from 0.6 to a failure threshold of 0.2 at 0.01 per day, RUL = (0.6 − 0.2) ÷ 0.01 = 40 days. Reliability models such as the Weibull distribution describe failure: R(t) = exp(−(t ÷ η)^β). With η = 1000 h and β = 2, R(500 h) = exp(−0.25) = 0.779. A β above 1 indicates wear-out.

Condition monitoring uses physics: a rolling bearing's outer-race defect frequency is BPFO = (n ÷ 2) f_r (1 − (d ÷ D) cos φ). With n = 9 balls, shaft speed f_r = 30 Hz, d ÷ D = 0.2 and φ = 0: BPFO = 4.5 × 30 × 0.8 = 108 Hz. A spectrum peak at 108 Hz and its harmonics suggests an outer-race fault. Sampling must satisfy the Nyquist criterion, at least twice the highest frequency of interest; for content up to 1 kHz, sample above 2 kHz.

Decisions and risks: alarm thresholds trade missed failures against false alarms and unnecessary stops; models must be updated as the asset changes; sensors and communications can fail; and data security matters because a twin can reveal operations or be attacked. A digital twin is only as good as its validation: check it against measured behaviour, record uncertainty and keep a human responsible for safety-critical decisions. Benefits include fewer unplanned stops, safer working and less waste, but only when predictions are trusted for good reasons.

stages.title: Integrated mechanical design and manufacturing project
stages.hook: You are asked to design a hoist for a workshop: lift 500 kg at 0.2 m/s, be safe, be buildable and be affordable. Where do you even begin, and how do you know when you are done?
explain: An integrated project joins everything: requirements, concepts, analysis, manufacturing, testing and lifecycle. A structured process helps: state requirements with measurable targets; generate concepts; select with a weighted decision matrix; do first-order calculations; check failure modes; design for manufacture and assembly; prototype and test; and plan maintenance and end of life. Each step can send you back.

First-order sizing for the hoist: lifting power at the load P = m g v = 500 × 9.8 × 0.2 = 980 W. With an overall efficiency of 0.8, the motor must supply 980 ÷ 0.8 = 1225 W, so a 1.5 kW motor is a sensible standard size. For a drum of 0.2 m diameter, ω = v ÷ r = 0.2 ÷ 0.1 = 2 rad/s = 19.1 rpm; a 1500 rpm motor needs a total reduction of 1500 ÷ 19.1 ≈ 78.5. Drum torque is m g r = 500 × 9.8 × 0.1 = 490 N m. A wire rope with a safety factor of 5 must have a minimum breaking load of at least 5 × 4900 = 24.5 kN.

A weighted decision matrix compares concepts. With criteria safety (weight 0.5), cost (0.3) and maintainability (0.2): concept A scores 8, 6 and 7, giving 0.5 × 8 + 0.3 × 6 + 0.2 × 7 = 7.2; concept B scores 6, 9 and 8, giving 3 + 2.7 + 1.6 = 7.3. The matrix is a conversation tool, so test how sensitive the ranking is to the weights.

Critical decisions are safety-driven: a lifting appliance needs an independent brake that holds the load on power loss, overload protection, limit switches, a rope inspection plan, an emergency stop and clear markings, following the relevant standards and legal requirements. Failure analysis (FMEA) ranks risks by severity, occurrence and detection. Design for manufacture simplifies parts and chooses standard components. Verification checks that the design meets requirements (calculations, FEA, tests), while validation checks that it meets the user's real need. Document assumptions, test results and limits, and take responsibility for the design's consequences.

steps: Output power = 500 × 9.8 × 0.2 = 980 W; motor power = 980 ÷ 0.8 = 1225 W.
Drum speed: ω = v ÷ r = 0.2 ÷ 0.1 = 2 rad/s = 2 × 60 ÷ (2π) = 19.1 rpm.

Designing so parts are easy and cheap to make and assemble.

misc.wrong: The best design is the one with the highest score in the decision matrix.
misc.right: The matrix guides discussion. Safety requirements are constraints that must be met, not traded off against cost.

stages.limits: First-order calculations are for sizing. Final design needs detailed analysis, standards compliance and testing.

trip.prompt: Find the V-model diagram. Match each design stage to the test that checks it.

questions.q: What is the difference between verification and validation?
o: Verification checks the design meets specs; validation checks it meets the real need
They are two names for the same check, which is done once at the end of the project
Validation is calculation only
Verification is marketing
questions.why: You can build the thing right and still build the wrong thing.

questions.q: A hoist lifts 500 kg at 0.2 m/s. What is the useful lifting power in watts? Use g = 9.8 m/s².
The drum radius is 0.1 m and the load is 500 kg. What torque is needed at the drum in N m? Use g = 9.8 m/s².
A wire rope must have a safety factor of 5 for a 4900 N load. What minimum breaking load is needed, in kN?
Concept A scores 8, 6, 7 and concept B scores 6, 9, 8 on safety (0.5), cost (0.3) and maintainability (0.2). Which has the higher weighted score?
o: B with 7.3
A with 7.2
Equal
Neither can be scored

questions.q: Concept B scores very low on safety (3) but wins on cost. What does a sound engineer do?
o: Reject or redesign it, because safety is a requirement not a trade-off
Choose B anyway, since cost decides the winner
Remove the safety row from the table
Hide the low score from the customer
questions.why: Minimum safety is a constraint; scoring is for comparing acceptable options.

questions.q: The hoist motor loses power mid-lift. What must happen?
o: An independent brake holds the load
The load falls slowly to the ground
The rope releases itself from the drum
The controller restarts the motor by itself
questions.why: A fail-safe brake that engages on power loss is a basic lifting requirement.

questions.q: Which action best checks that the finished hoist meets the user's real need?
o: Trial in the workshop with real users and loads under supervision
Calculating the design again several times on paper with a safety factor
Another meeting
Changing the paint
questions.why: Validation uses real use conditions, not only calculations.

questions.q: List four activities you would include in a plan that takes the hoist from concept to a safe in-service product.
questions.model: Write measurable requirements; size components by calculation and analysis; run FMEA or hazard analysis; build a prototype and proof-load test it; plan manufacture and assembly; and set up inspection, maintenance, training and compliance with lifting standards.
questions.why: A safe product needs analysis, testing, manufacture and lifecycle planning.

questions.q: Match each project stage to its main output.
questions.why: Each stage produces something the next stage uses.

panel.q: A proof test of 1.25 times the rated load is applied before a hoist enters service. What is its purpose?
o: To confirm the structure and brake hold with a margin before use
To wear the hoist in so that its parts settle into the shape they will keep
To make it look new
To lower the load rating
panel.why: Proof testing verifies safe capacity and reveals defects, within standard limits.

panel.q: Cost pressure pushes the team to use a lower grade of rope with a safety factor of 3.5 against a requirement of 5. What is the correct step?
o: Keep the requirement; find savings elsewhere or change the requirement only through proper approval
Quietly use the cheaper rope, since 3.5 is close enough to 5 and no one will notice
Remove the proof test from the plan so the rope's real rating is never measured
Mark the rope as 5
panel.why: Safety requirements cannot be eroded to save cost; changes need formal justification and approval.

panel.q: After delivery, the supplier learns a batch of rope is under-strength. What is the ethical obligation?
o: Inform users promptly and recall or replace the affected parts
Say nothing, since no one has been hurt yet
Wait for a failure before taking any action
Blame the user for overloading the equipment
panel.why: Engineering ethics puts public safety first and requires prompt disclosure.

teach.topic: How to turn a need into a safe design
teach.model: Start with measurable requirements, such as lift 500 kg at 0.2 m/s. Generate concepts and compare them, but treat safety as a constraint, not a score to trade off. Size the motor, gearing and rope with first-order calculations, check the failure modes, prototype and test, and plan maintenance. Verification checks the design meets the specification, and validation checks it meets the real need.

points.ask: Where do you start?
How do you choose between ideas?
How do you check it will work and be safe?
How do you know you're done?
